questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Anyone who has tried to hold a conversation beside a busy road knows the instinctive remedy: you raise your voice, and perhaps its pitch, until you are heard. Birds, it turns out, do something similar. In many cities, songbirds of several species sing at a higher pitch than their relatives in the quieter countryside, apparently lifting their songs clear of the low rumble of traffic. Some sing more loudly; some start earlier, before the morning rush begins; a few have taken to singing at night, when the streets are quieter.

It is tempting to read such findings as evolution caught in the act, and headlines have rarely resisted the temptation. Cities are young, the argument runs, so any trait that sets urban populations apart must have arisen at remarkable speed. The story appeals because it turns the city, usually cast as nature's enemy, into a laboratory in which natural selection can be watched at work.

The trouble is that a difference between two populations says nothing, on its own, about how the difference came about. A bird that sings higher in a city may carry genes that its rural cousins lack, but it may equally be an ordinary bird doing what birds of its kind have always been able to do: adjusting its song to its surroundings, much as we adjust our voices in a crowded restaurant. Individual birds of some species have been observed raising and lowering their pitch as the noise around them rises and falls, which is hard to square with the idea of a fixed, inherited trait. Telling the two explanations apart requires patient work—raising birds from different populations under identical conditions, for instance—and such studies are slow, expensive and, by the standards of a news cycle, unexciting.

None of this makes urban song less interesting. If anything, the case for flexibility raises a sharper question. Many species have never settled in cities at all, while others have moved in with apparent ease. Perhaps what distinguishes the successful newcomers is not a change acquired after arrival but a capacity they brought with them: a readiness to vary their behaviour when circumstances change. On this view, the city does not so much create new kinds of birds as sort existing ones, admitting those that were adaptable to begin with and quietly turning the rest away.

That is a less dramatic story than evolution at high speed, but it may prove the more useful one. If flexibility is the price of admission, then the species we should worry about as cities spread are not those that already share our streets, but those whose habits are too fixed to follow.
options: Traffic noise has forced urban songbirds to evolve higher-pitched songs in a remarkably short time.
Only slow and patient research can show whether city birds really sing differently from rural ones.
The way city birds sing may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change.
City birds may have evolved their flexible way of singing as a response to urban noise.
questions.explain: The author grants that urban birds sing differently but argues that the difference 'says nothing, on its own' about its cause, that it may equally reflect birds adjusting their song, and that such adaptability may also explain which species manage to settle in cities at all, so the songs may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change. The idea that traffic noise has forced rapid evolution is the headline reading the author questions. The suggestion that birds evolved their flexibility in response to city noise contradicts the text, which presents flexibility as 'a capacity they brought with them', not 'a change acquired after arrival'. Patient research is said to be needed to tell the two explanations apart, not to establish whether city birds sing differently, which the text treats as an observed fact.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the author, can closer inspection not solve the main problem?
questions.passage:
Every organisation that tries to manage by numbers sooner or later runs into the same awkward fact. A figure that once told you something useful about how well people were working starts, the moment you reward or punish them according to it, to tell you mainly how good they have become at producing that figure. Economists call this Goodhart's law, after the British economist who described it, but few of us need the name. We have all heard of call centres that time their calls and end up with staff who cut difficult customers off, or of schools judged on exam results that quietly stop entering pupils who might fail.

The usual response is outrage, followed by tighter rules. On this account the trouble is cheating: a few unscrupulous individuals game the system, and the cure is closer inspection. Cheating certainly happens, but it is not the heart of the problem. Far more common, and far harder to detect, is the conscientious employee who simply does what she has been asked. Told that her performance will be judged on a single number, she devotes her limited time and attention to that number, and the parts of her job that nobody counts—the patient explanation, the colleague helped out of a tight spot—shrink without anyone ever deciding that they should. No rule has been broken. That is precisely why inspection cannot fix it.

It does not follow that we should throw our measurements away. Organisations that abandon numbers altogether tend to fall back on impressions, and impressions are hardly free of bias; they favour the confident, the visible and the familiar. A hospital that stops recording waiting times does not thereby become kinder to its patients. The question is not whether to measure but what to do with the measurements once we have them.

Here a distinction that is often blurred in practice becomes useful. A number can serve as the start of a conversation or as a verdict. In the first case, a sudden drop in a team's figures prompts someone to go and find out what is happening, and the answer may well be that the team is doing something valuable that the number cannot see. In the second, the same drop sets off an automatic penalty, and the team learns to protect the number rather than explain it. The figures are identical in both cases; what differs is whether anyone is still expected to exercise judgement.

Such judgement does not come cheap. It requires managers who understand the work well enough to see what the numbers leave out, and it cannot be scaled up as easily as a spreadsheet. But the alternative is not objectivity. It is an organisation that knows more and more about less and less.
options: Because conscientious employees hide from inspectors the parts of the job they neglect
Because the problem lies in what people are asked to do, not in people breaking rules
Because inspectors tend to favour the confident, the visible and the familiar
Because cheating has become far too widespread to be investigated properly
questions.explain: The author argues that the main problem is not cheating but the conscientious employee who 'simply does what she has been asked', concentrating on the number she is judged by while the uncounted parts of the job shrink; no rule is broken, which is 'precisely why inspection cannot fix it'. This behaviour is 'far harder to detect' because nothing is being broken, not because employees hide what they neglect; the text says the shrinking happens 'without anyone ever deciding that they should'. The bias towards the confident, the visible and the familiar is attributed to impressions, not to inspectors. And the claim that cheating is too widespread contradicts the statement that cheating 'is not the heart of the problem'.

questions.prompt: In the fourth paragraph, what distinguishes using a number as 'the start of a conversation' from using it as 'a verdict'?
questions.passage:
Every organisation that tries to manage by numbers sooner or later runs into the same awkward fact. A figure that once told you something useful about how well people were working starts, the moment you reward or punish them according to it, to tell you mainly how good they have become at producing that figure. Economists call this Goodhart's law, after the British economist who described it, but few of us need the name. We have all heard of call centres that time their calls and end up with staff who cut difficult customers off, or of schools judged on exam results that quietly stop entering pupils who might fail.

The usual response is outrage, followed by tighter rules. On this account the trouble is cheating: a few unscrupulous individuals game the system, and the cure is closer inspection. Cheating certainly happens, but it is not the heart of the problem. Far more common, and far harder to detect, is the conscientious employee who simply does what she has been asked. Told that her performance will be judged on a single number, she devotes her limited time and attention to that number, and the parts of her job that nobody counts—the patient explanation, the colleague helped out of a tight spot—shrink without anyone ever deciding that they should. No rule has been broken. That is precisely why inspection cannot fix it.

It does not follow that we should throw our measurements away. Organisations that abandon numbers altogether tend to fall back on impressions, and impressions are hardly free of bias; they favour the confident, the visible and the familiar. A hospital that stops recording waiting times does not thereby become kinder to its patients. The question is not whether to measure but what to do with the measurements once we have them.

In the first case, a sudden drop in a team's figures prompts someone to go and find out what is happening, and the answer may well be that the team is doing something valuable that the number cannot see. In the second, the same drop sets off an automatic penalty, and the team learns to protect the number rather than explain it. options: Whether a drop in the figures is looked into or punished automatically
Whether the figures are discussed openly with the staff or kept among the managers
Whether the figures are accurate or have been quietly manipulated by the team itself
Whether the figures describe the performance of individual employees or of whole teams
questions.explain: The author explains that a number used as the start of a conversation makes someone 'go and find out what is happening', whereas a number used as a verdict 'sets off an automatic penalty'; what differs is 'whether anyone is still expected to exercise judgement'. The word 'conversation' does not refer to sharing figures with staff rather than managers, and nothing is said about who sees the numbers. Both cases concern the same team's figures, so the distinction is not between individuals and teams.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage: In a famous passage of his Confessions, Augustine describes watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, at his reading: his eyes ran over the page and his heart searched out the meaning, but his voice and tongue were still. For generations the scene was cited as proof that silent reading was a rarity in the ancient world—an oddity worth writing down. The inference is weaker than it looks. Ambrose was not alone in a study when Augustine saw him; he read in this way while visitors sat waiting to speak with him. And Augustine's own guesses at the reason—that the bishop wished to avoid being asked to explain difficult passages to his listeners, or to spare a voice that tired easily—concern why a man would read silently in company, not whether such reading was possible. A single surprised witness, in any case, tells us first of all about the witness's own expectations. Whether those expectations were shared by everyone who could read is another question.
options: Silent reading may well have been rarer in antiquity than modern scholars tend to assume.
Augustine misunderstood the reasons why Ambrose chose to read in silence.
Silent reading was in fact widespread in the ancient world, as Augustine's account shows.
Augustine's account says less about ancient reading habits than is often assumed.
questions.explain: The author's central claim is that 'the inference is weaker than it looks': the scene has long been cited as proof that silent reading was rare, but the circumstances and Augustine's own guesses suggest that it shows something narrower. The suggestion that silent reading may have been rarer than modern scholars assume runs against this argument, which weakens the evidence for rarity rather than strengthening it. Nor does the text claim that Augustine misunderstood Ambrose's reasons; his guesses are used as evidence of what puzzled him. Finally, the author does not argue that silent reading was widespread, since whether Augustine's expectations were shared by other readers is left as 'another question'.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why may a document saved thirty years ago be impossible to read today?
questions.passage: A letter left in a drawer for three hundred years can usually still be read by anyone who knows the language. A document saved on a computer thirty years ago may be beyond rescue even if the disk that holds it is in perfect condition. The bits survive; what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them—the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system. Each layer was built on the unspoken assumption that the one beneath it would always be there. Seen this way, preserving digital material has less in common with storing objects than with keeping a language in use. Putting files somewhere safe is only the beginning; someone must go on carrying them over into forms that the tools of the day can open, again and again, for as long as anyone wants them read. A digital archive, in other words, is less a place than an activity.
options: The data on the disk fades gradually, even when the disk itself is well kept.
Modern computers are designed to refuse files made on much older systems.
The programs and machines needed to open it may no longer exist.
No one may still remember what the document was originally for.
questions.explain: The text says that 'the bits survive' and that what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them: 'the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system'. The idea that the data fades contradicts this, as well as the statement that the disk may be in perfect condition. Nothing is said about modern computers being designed to refuse old files; the problem is that the layers needed to read them have disappeared. And 'make sense of them' refers to these technical layers, not to people forgetting what a document was for.

questions.prompt: What does the author suggest about the queue outside such a restaurant?
questions.passage: Restaurants that refuse to take bookings like to present the policy as a kind of democracy: no favours for those with connections, first come, first served. The economics are less high-minded. A reserved table that nobody turns up to claim is pure loss, and on a busy night a handful of no-shows can wipe out the profit from an entire sitting. Abolishing reservations moves that risk elsewhere. Instead of the restaurant waiting for diners who may never arrive, the diners wait for tables that are certain to come free—and they do so on the pavement, in full view of everyone walking past. Few forms of advertising are as persuasive as a line of people willing to stand in the rain for their dinner, and this one costs nothing. Customers are not necessarily the losers, of course; plenty of them would rather queue for half an hour than plan a meal three weeks ahead. But it is worth being clear about whom the arrangement was designed to serve.
options: It shows that many diners find the policy more frustrating than they admit.
It works in the restaurant's favour by catching the eye of passers-by.
It is a reliable sign that the food is better than at restaurants nearby.
It tends to discourage people walking past from trying the restaurant.
questions.explain: The author says that few forms of advertising are as persuasive as a line of people willing to stand in the rain, and adds that 'this one costs nothing', so the queue benefits the restaurant by attracting attention. The text does not say that the food really is better; the queue persuades passers-by, but nothing is said about whether that impression is accurate. Saying that the queue puts people off reverses the author's point. And the author notes that 'plenty' of customers would rather queue than book weeks ahead, which does not fit the idea that diners are secretly frustrated.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the text?
questions.passage: Few scientific images have travelled as far as the 'wood wide web'. The phrase describes the threads of soil fungi that link the roots of neighbouring trees, and in popular retellings it has grown into something close to a forest internet, through which old 'mother trees' feed their seedlings and warn their neighbours of danger. The fungal connections themselves are real, and remarkable. What is less secure is the story told about them. Showing that carbon or a chemical signal passes from one tree to another is hard enough in the field; showing that it travelled through the fungus rather than through the soil, and that the transfer makes any difference to the tree that receives it, is harder still. Several researchers have recently argued that the evidence for the most popular claims is thinner than books and documentaries suggest. That is no reason to stop marvelling at the forest floor. It is a reason to notice when a metaphor has begun to do the work that evidence should be doing.
options: A Story That Has Outrun the Science
The Wood Wide Web Exposed as a Myth
How Old Trees Care for Their Young
The Hidden Network Beneath Our Forests
questions.explain: The author accepts that the fungal connections are 'real, and remarkable' but argues that 'the story told about them' goes beyond what has been shown, ending with a warning about a metaphor doing 'the work that evidence should be doing', which is what 'A Story That Has Outrun the Science' expresses. A title claiming that the wood wide web has been exposed as a myth is too strong, since the connections themselves are said to be real. A title about old trees caring for their young repeats the popular claim that the author questions. A title about a hidden network names the topic but leaves out the author's point, which is a criticism of how that network has been described.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Few medical messages are as easy to sell as the promise of early detection. Find a disease before it causes symptoms, the reasoning goes, and you can treat it while it is still small, simple and curable. It is hard to imagine anyone objecting, and in public campaigns hardly anyone does. Yet the figures most often quoted in support of screening are among the least reliable guides to whether it works.

Consider survival rates: the share of patients still alive, say, five years after diagnosis. Imagine a woman whose tumour, left to announce itself, would cause symptoms at the age of 64 and kill her at 68. Her survival after diagnosis would be four years. Now suppose that a screening test finds the same tumour at 58, and that the treatment she then receives makes no difference whatever. She still dies at 68, but she has now survived ten years after diagnosis and counts as a five-year survivor. The statistics have improved; her life has not been extended by a single day. All that has changed is the moment at which the clock was started.

A second distortion is less obvious and, in some ways, more troubling. Screening does not only find dangerous diseases earlier. It also finds abnormalities that would never have caused any harm: tumours that grow so slowly, or stop growing altogether, that the people carrying them would have died of something else without ever knowing they were there. Doctors call this overdiagnosis. Its victims are turned into patients and given treatment—surgery, radiotherapy, years of check-ups—from which they cannot benefit, because there was nothing to cure. And since no one can tell, in any individual case, which tumours belonged to this harmless group, every one of these people has reason to believe that the test saved their life.

The result is a paradox. The more overdiagnosis a programme causes, the more survivors it produces, the more grateful patients it has to speak on its behalf, and the more popular it becomes. A programme that did nothing but harm could, in principle, earn a reputation as one of medicine's great successes.

None of this means that screening is a mistake. For some diseases, large trials in which people were invited to screening or not, at random, have shown that fewer of those invited went on to die of the disease. That, rather than survival after diagnosis, is the figure that matters, because neither distortion can flatter it: starting the clock earlier does not, by itself, postpone a single death, and finding harmless tumours does not prevent one. The difficulty is that such trials take many years and very large numbers of people, and their results are rarely as dramatic as the stories told by survivors.

What follows is not that people should refuse to be screened, but that they deserve to be told what they are being offered. An invitation that mentions only the lives saved, and not the healthy people turned into patients, is not really asking for consent. It is asking for applause.
options: Screening may well do more harm than good, since many of the tumours it finds would never have caused any harm.
The figures and stories most often cited in support of screening say little about whether it saves lives.
Survival rates mislead chiefly because screening programmes start counting from the moment a tumour is found.
Screening ought to be offered only for diseases where large trials have shown that it prevents deaths.
questions.explain: The author argues that survival figures can improve without anyone living longer, and that overdiagnosis creates grateful 'survivors' who were never in danger, so that even a programme that 'did nothing but harm' could look like a great success; the usual evidence therefore says little about whether screening saves lives. The idea that screening may do more harm than good runs against 'None of this means that screening is a mistake', and the text never says how many of the tumours found are harmless. Starting the count at diagnosis is only one of the two distortions described, and the text does not single it out as the chief one; it even calls the second 'in some ways, more troubling'. A single distortion is in any case too narrow to be the main point. Nor does the author say that screening should be restricted to diseases where trials have shown a benefit; the conclusion is that people deserve to be told what they are being offered.

Consider survival rates: the share of patients still alive, say, five years after diagnosis. Imagine a woman whose tumour, left to announce itself, would cause symptoms at the age of 64 and kill her at 68. Her survival after diagnosis would be four years. Now suppose that a screening test finds the same tumour at 58, and that the treatment she then receives makes no difference whatever. She still dies at 68, but she has now survived ten years after diagnosis and counts as a five-year survivor. The statistics have improved; her life has not been extended by a single day. All that has changed is the moment at which the clock was started.

A second distortion is less obvious and, in some ways, more troubling. Screening does not only find dangerous diseases earlier. It also finds abnormalities that would never have caused any harm: tumours that grow so slowly, or stop growing altogether, that the people carrying them would have died of something else without ever knowing they were there. Doctors call this overdiagnosis. Its victims are turned into patients and given treatment—surgery, radiotherapy, years of check-ups—from which they cannot benefit, because there was nothing to cure. And since no one can tell, in any individual case, which tumours belonged to this harmless group, every one of these people has reason to believe that the test saved their life.

The result is a paradox. The more overdiagnosis a programme causes, the more survivors it produces, the more grateful patients it has to speak on its behalf, and the more popular it becomes. A programme that did nothing but harm could, in principle, earn a reputation as one of medicine's great successes.

None of this means that screening is a mistake. For some diseases, large trials in which people were invited to screening or not, at random, have shown that fewer of those invited went on to die of the disease. That, rather than survival after diagnosis, is the figure that matters, because neither distortion can flatter it: starting the clock earlier does not, by itself, postpone a single death, and finding harmless tumours does not prevent one. The difficulty is that such trials take many years and very large numbers of people, and their results are rarely as dramatic as the stories told by survivors.

What follows is not that people should refuse to be screened, but that they deserve to be told what they are being offered. An invitation that mentions only the lives saved, and not the healthy people turned into patients, is not really asking for consent. It is asking for applause.

Screening tends to find tumours too late for treatment to change the outcome.
People whose tumours are found by screening are likely to live to an older age.
Survival after diagnosis can increase even when death comes no later.

questions.prompt: According to the reviewer, what is the novel's greatest strength?
questions.passage:
Halfway through this first novel, its fifteen-year-old narrator watches her father wash the family car three times in a single afternoon. Nell does not know why he is doing it, and the novel does not stop to explain. It is the last week before the fish-processing plant where he has worked for twenty years closes its doors, and the reader grasps at once what she cannot: that a man who will soon have nowhere to go in the morning needs something to do with his hands. Nell notices only that the car has never been so clean.

Scenes like this are the novel's great strength. The closure of the plant, which employs half the town, is the largest event in the book, yet it happens almost entirely offstage. We glimpse it in telephone calls overheard through a bedroom floor, in a neighbour's sudden wish to sell her piano, in the disappearance of the smell that used to hang over the harbour. Nell is far more interested in a boy from the campsite than in redundancy payments, and through her the catastrophe arrives as a series of small puzzles. The effect is not to make the town's loss seem smaller but to make it sharper. We are always a step ahead of the narrator, and it is in the space between what she sees and what we understand that the novel does its work.

The prose is plain, almost to a fault. There are few metaphors and fewer adjectives, and some readers will find the opening chapters slow. They should persist. The plainness turns out to be a kind of tact: a more colourful style would have crowded out the reader, who is being asked, page after page, to supply what Nell leaves out.

The trouble begins in the final third. Having kept us at Nell's shoulder for two hundred pages, the author suddenly hands the story to the father, in a series of chapters that tell us what he was thinking on the afternoon of the car and on all the others. Nothing in them is false, and some of it is moving. But very little of it is news. We had understood him perfectly well through his daughter's incomprehension; to have him explained is to be told what we had already worked out for ourselves, and to lose the very gap that had given the book its force. First novels are usually faulted for putting too much in. This one's fault is subtler: its author seems not to trust that she has already put enough in.

The ending, in which a new employer arrives, the father finds work and nobody has to leave, is tidier than anything that precedes it. One can see the impulse—after so much quiet loss, the author wants to give her characters something—but tidiness is an odd reward for a book whose great virtue was its willingness to leave things unsaid. Still, the first two-thirds are as fine as anything I have read this year, and a writer who can sustain that kind of restraint for so long will surely learn to sustain it to the last page.
options: Its detailed account of how the closure of the plant affects the town's economy
Its use of the father's point of view to explain what his daughter cannot see
The way it allows readers to understand more than its young narrator does
The vivid and colourful language in which the town and its people are described
questions.explain: The reviewer calls scenes like the one with the car 'the novel's great strength' and explains that 'we are always a step ahead of the narrator': the book does its work in the space between what Nell sees and what the reader understands. The closure is said to happen 'almost entirely offstage', so the book gives no detailed account of its economic effects. The chapters told from the father's point of view are what the reviewer criticises, not praises. And the prose is described as 'plain, almost to a fault', with few metaphors and fewer adjectives.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the text, do linguists see a child's use of 'goed' as progress?
questions.passage: Parents are sometimes alarmed when a child who has been saying 'went' and 'ran' for months starts to say 'goed' and 'runned'. It looks like a step backwards. Linguists see it the other way round. A two-year-old who says 'went' may simply be repeating a word she has heard, much as she repeats the names of her toys. A three-year-old who says 'goed' is doing something more ambitious. She has noticed that most English verbs form their past tense by adding the same ending, and she has begun to apply that pattern even to verbs that do not follow it. Hardly anyone around her says 'goed', so she has not simply copied it; she has built it herself. In time she will learn which verbs are exceptions, and 'went' will win out again—this time not as an isolated word but as a known exception to a rule she has mastered. The temporary dip, in other words, is not a sign of decline. It is the sound of a grammar being built.
options: It shows that she has begun to learn which verbs are exceptions.
It shows that she is learning more from other children than from adults.
It shows that she has started to correct the mistakes she made at two.
It shows that she has found a regularity and is extending it by herself.
questions.explain: The child who says 'goed' has noticed that most verbs form the past tense with the same ending and has begun to apply that pattern even to verbs that do not follow it, building the form 'herself'; this shows that she is working out rules rather than repeating what she hears. Learning which verbs are exceptions comes later, when 'went' wins out again. The text says that she has not simply copied the form, and it says nothing about learning from other children. Nor is she correcting earlier mistakes, since at two she said 'went', which is correct.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what did the safety brake and its public demonstration achieve?
questions.passage:
The passenger lift is often described as the invention that made the skyscraper possible, but lifting people was never the difficult part. Hoists of one kind or another had carried goods up and down buildings for centuries. What kept people off them was the fear of what would happen if the rope broke. The decisive step, taken in the 1850s, was a safety brake that locked the platform to its guide rails the moment the rope went slack—together with a public demonstration in which its inventor stood on a raised platform and ordered the rope to be cut. What he was selling, in other words, was not a way of going up but a reason to believe that one would not come down too fast.

The consequences reached far beyond engineering. In a building without a lift, the upper floors were the least desirable: every visit meant another flight of stairs, and the rooms under the roof went to servants and to those who could afford nothing better. Once the lift made height effortless, that order was turned upside down. The top floor, long the cheapest in the building, became the most expensive, and height, once a burden, became something people were willing to pay for.
options: They gave people a reason to trust a kind of machine that already existed.
They made it possible for the first time to raise goods to the top of tall buildings.
They replaced the rope with a mechanism that could not break.
They allowed lifts to travel much faster than earlier hoists had done.
questions.explain: The text says that lifting 'was never the difficult part', since hoists had existed for centuries; what kept people off them was fear, and the brake and the demonstration gave them 'a reason to believe that one would not come down too fast'. Raising goods to the top of buildings was nothing new, as the old hoists show. The rope was not replaced: the brake worked when the rope went slack, and the demonstration involved cutting it. Nothing is said about how fast lifts travelled; 'too fast' refers to falling, not to the lift's normal speed.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Walk through almost any city park and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass where the paved path takes a longer way round. Planners call them desire paths, and for a long time the standard response was to discourage them with a fence, a hedge or a sign asking people to keep to the path. More recently, a humbler view has gained ground. A desire path, on this view, is not vandalism but information: a record, written by thousands of feet, of where people actually want to go, and therefore of a mistake in the original design. questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Every spring, volunteers in parks and nature reserves across much of Europe spend their weekends pulling up plants that are judged not to belong. The work is often described in military language. Unwanted species are 'invaders' or 'aliens'; they 'colonise' riverbanks and 'conquer' woodland; the volunteers who uproot them are fighting a 'war'. The vocabulary is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a choice, and one that carries an argument within it: that a species which arrived with human help is, for that reason alone, an enemy.

Some introduced species have certainly earned the hostility. When the brown tree snake reached the Pacific island of Guam, probably as a stowaway in military cargo shortly after the Second World War, it found an abundance of birds that had never had to deal with a climbing predator. Within a few decades most of the island's native forest birds had disappeared. Stories like this are the reason why biologists take introductions seriously, and they are not rare.

They are, however, unrepresentative. Of all the species that people carry to new places, deliberately or by accident, the great majority fail to survive in the wild at all. Of those that do survive, most remain local and unremarkable, and only a small fraction go on to spread widely and cause serious harm. Ecologists have long used a rough rule of thumb according to which only about one species in ten passes each of these stages. The figures vary greatly from one group of organisms to another, but the general pattern holds: being non-native is common, and being harmful is not. A label that applies equally to the brown tree snake and to a garden flower that has quietly grown in a few hedgerows for two centuries tells us very little about either.

The label is also less precise than it sounds. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some point in time, but which point? In Britain, botanists treat plants that arrived before about 1500 more or less as natives, and several well-loved cornfield flowers would fail a stricter test. As the climate warms, the question becomes harder still. Species are now shifting their ranges northwards without anyone's help, and it is not obvious whether a butterfly that crosses the Channel under its own power should be welcomed as a refugee or resisted as an intruder. Meanwhile, some undoubtedly native species do great damage when circumstances change: deer, freed from the predators that people removed long ago, can strip a woodland of its young trees as thoroughly as any newcomer.

None of this means that origin is irrelevant. A species that evolved elsewhere has not been tested against the predators, parasites and competitors it will meet in its new home, and the consequences of its arrival are therefore harder to predict. Moreover, prevention is far cheaper than cure. Once a species has become established over a wide area, removing it may be impossible at any price, while checking cargo and banning the sale of risky plants costs relatively little. At the border, then, treating unfamiliar species with suspicion is simply prudent.

The mistake is to carry the same reasoning into places where it no longer applies. A plant that has lived in a region for a hundred years is no longer an unknown quantity; its effects can be observed rather than guessed at. If it crowds out other species, damages riverbanks or poisons livestock, there is a case for controlling it. If it does none of these things, the fact that it came from somewhere else is not, by itself, a reason to spend scarce money and volunteer time on removing it, money and time that might be used against a native species that is doing real harm.

What the military vocabulary obscures is that conservation is ultimately about choices: which landscapes we want, which losses we are prepared to accept, and where limited resources will do the most good. Asking where a species came from is a useful first question. Treating it as the last one turns a matter of judgement into a matter of identity, and that is rarely a good basis for any decision.
options: Military language has made the public more hostile to introduced species than most biologists are.
Introduced species are rarely harmful, so money spent on controlling them would do more good elsewhere.
A species' origin is a better guide to keeping new species out than to dealing with established ones.
The idea of a native species has lost its meaning now that a warming climate is moving species around.
questions.explain: The author accepts that suspicion of unfamiliar species is 'simply prudent' at the border, since newcomers are unpredictable and prevention is cheap, but argues that a species which has lived in a region for a long time should be judged by its observed effects, not by where it came from: origin is 'a useful first question' but should not be the last. The text does say that most introduced species are harmless, but the conclusion that money spent on controlling them would be better used elsewhere goes too far: the author supports checking cargo and banning risky plants, and says there is a case for controlling an established plant that does harm. Nothing suggests that biologists are less hostile than the public; the text says they 'take introductions seriously'. And although a warming climate makes the question of what is native 'harder still', the author does not conclude that the idea has lost its meaning, but goes on to defend origin as relevant at the border.

Unwanted species are 'invaders' or 'aliens'; they 'colonise' riverbanks and 'conquer' woodland; the volunteers who uproot them are fighting a 'war'. The vocabulary is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a choice, and one that carries an argument within it: that a species which arrived with human help is, for that reason alone, an enemy.

Some introduced species have certainly earned the hostility. When the brown tree snake reached the Pacific island of Guam, probably as a stowaway in military cargo shortly after the Second World War, it found an abundance of birds that had never had to deal with a climbing predator. Within a few decades most of the island's native forest birds had disappeared. Stories like this are the reason why biologists take introductions seriously, and they are not rare.

They are, however, unrepresentative. Of all the species that people carry to new places, deliberately or by accident, the great majority fail to survive in the wild at all. Of those that do survive, most remain local and unremarkable, and only a small fraction go on to spread widely and cause serious harm. Ecologists have long used a rough rule of thumb according to which only about one species in ten passes each of these stages. The figures vary greatly from one group of organisms to another, but the general pattern holds: being non-native is common, and being harmful is not. A label that applies equally to the brown tree snake and to a garden flower that has quietly grown in a few hedgerows for two centuries tells us very little about either.

The label is also less precise than it sounds. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some point in time, but which point? In Britain, botanists treat plants that arrived before about 1500 more or less as natives, and several well-loved cornfield flowers would fail a stricter test. As the climate warms, the question becomes harder still. Species are now shifting their ranges northwards without anyone's help, and it is not obvious whether a butterfly that crosses the Channel under its own power should be welcomed as a refugee or resisted as an intruder. Meanwhile, some undoubtedly native species do great damage when circumstances change: deer, freed from the predators that people removed long ago, can strip a woodland of its young trees as thoroughly as any newcomer.

None of this means that origin is irrelevant. A species that evolved elsewhere has not been tested against the predators, parasites and competitors it will meet in its new home, and the consequences of its arrival are therefore harder to predict. Moreover, prevention is far cheaper than cure. Once a species has become established over a wide area, removing it may be impossible at any price, while checking cargo and banning the sale of risky plants costs relatively little. At the border, then, treating unfamiliar species with suspicion is simply prudent.

The mistake is to carry the same reasoning into places where it no longer applies. A plant that has lived in a region for a hundred years is no longer an unknown quantity; its effects can be observed rather than guessed at. If it crowds out other species, damages riverbanks or poisons livestock, there is a case for controlling it. If it does none of these things, the fact that it came from somewhere else is not, by itself, a reason to spend scarce money and volunteer time on removing it, money and time that might be used against a native species that is doing real harm.

What the military vocabulary obscures is that conservation is ultimately about choices: which landscapes we want, which losses we are prepared to accept, and where limited resources will do the most good. Asking where a species came from is a useful first question. Treating it as the last one turns a matter of judgement into a matter of identity, and that is rarely a good basis for any decision.
options: Conservationists tend to identify too closely with the native species they protect.
Only experts, not volunteers, are able to judge where a species really comes from.
A species would then be condemned for what it is rather than for what it actually does.
A species gradually takes on a new identity once it has lived in a region long enough.
questions.explain: The author has argued that decisions about established species should rest on weighing their actual effects and the best use of limited resources, which is 'a matter of judgement'. Deciding solely on the basis of where a species came from would instead make its fate depend on what it is, its 'identity', regardless of whether it does any harm. The text says nothing about conservationists identifying with native species, or about experts and volunteers differing in their ability to determine origins. And although a long-established plant is said to be 'no longer an unknown quantity', the author does not claim that its identity changes; the point is that its effects can now be observed.

questions.prompt: What does the reviewer appreciate about Coyle's portrayal of Robert FitzRoy?
questions.passage:
Weather forecasts are among the few scientific predictions that most of us consult every day, and among the few we feel entitled to mock. Harriet Coyle's Tomorrow's Sky, a history of the forecast from the first newspaper predictions to the present, sets out to explain how something so routine came to be possible, and why it still so often feels unreliable.

The book is at its best in its first half, which follows a handful of people who tried to predict the weather before anyone was sure it could be done. Coyle is particularly good on Robert FitzRoy, the naval officer who began publishing daily forecasts in The Times in 1861 and was mocked in the press whenever they failed. She resists the temptation to make him a martyr to science. Her FitzRoy is stubborn and thin-skinned, as quick to blame his critics as his instruments, and all the more sympathetic for it. Equally memorable is her account of Lewis Fry Richardson, who during the First World War spent weeks working out by hand a forecast for a single six-hour period, using the kind of physical equations that computers now solve. His result was wildly wrong, and Coyle shows with real skill why the failure was more instructive than many successes: his method was sound, but the data and the arithmetic available to him were not up to it.

The trouble begins when the story reaches the age in which the method finally worked. The arrival of satellites and electronic computers, which turned a speculative craft into a reliable service, is covered in a single chapter, and a hurried one. A reader would learn more from a few pages of a decent textbook about how today's forecasts are actually made. It is hard not to suspect that Coyle simply finds the earlier period more congenial: it has more eccentrics in it, and fewer committees.

That preference also shapes the argument that runs through the book. Coyle's central claim is that the history of forecasting is a history of learning to be uncertain. Early forecasters offered confident statements and were ridiculed when these turned out wrong; their modern successors speak of a seventy per cent chance of rain, and in doing so tell us something more honest about what can be known. It is an attractive idea, and in places a genuinely illuminating one. But it is repeated so often, and applied to so many episodes, that it begins to look less like a conclusion than a lens fitted before the evidence was examined. Forecasters did not, after all, begin to express themselves in probabilities simply because they became more modest. They did so in large part because they acquired the means of calculating those probabilities, and those means are exactly what the hurried chapter leaves out.

Coyle writes clear and often elegant prose, though she is too fond of meteorological metaphor; by the time a disagreement between two committees had been described as 'a cold front moving through the department', this reader was longing for plainer language. Such lapses are minor. The larger problem is one of balance, and it is a pity, because the material she has chosen to dwell on is handled with real distinction.

Tomorrow's Sky is, in the end, a fine book about the past of forecasting and a thin one about its present. Readers who want to know why the forecast on their phone is so much better than it was a generation ago will have to look elsewhere. Those who want to know why anyone attempted it in the first place could hardly do better.
options: It shows how unfairly the press treated a pioneer of science.
It presents him as a flawed man rather than as a heroic victim.
It explains why his forecasts were better than his critics thought.
It shows that his stubbornness was the key to his later success.
questions.explain: The reviewer praises Coyle for resisting 'the temptation to make him a martyr to science': her FitzRoy is 'stubborn and thin-skinned' and 'all the more sympathetic for it', so he appears as a man with faults rather than as a heroic victim. Saying that the book shows how unfairly the press treated him reverses this point, since portraying him as wronged by his critics is exactly the martyr's story Coyle avoids. The review does not say that his forecasts were better than his critics believed, and his stubbornness is presented as a flaw of character, not as the reason for any success.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Anyone who has spent a night on a hospital ward will remember the noise. Monitors beep when a patient's heart rate rises or falls, infusion pumps chime when a bag runs empty, and sensors sound when a clip slips off a finger. Each of these alarms exists for a good reason, and each was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer. Taken together, however, they may be doing the opposite.

The problem is not that alarms fail to go off, but that they go off far too often. Studies of intensive care units have repeatedly found that most alarms require no action at all: the patient has moved, a cable has come loose, or a reading has briefly crossed a limit and returned to normal of its own accord. Staff who hear hundreds of such signals in a shift learn, quite reasonably, that an alarm usually means nothing. They respond more slowly, silence devices without checking, or widen the limits until the machines fall quiet. Nurses call this alarm fatigue, and it has been linked to cases in which a genuine emergency went unnoticed because the signal announcing it sounded exactly like the hundred false ones that preceded it.

What makes the problem stubborn is that no one is responsible for it. A manufacturer who sets a monitor to sound at the slightest irregularity is protected if something goes wrong; a manufacturer who sets it to stay quiet is not. Every individual decision to add an alarm, or to make one more sensitive, is easy to defend. The total, which is what the nurse actually has to live with, is no one's decision at all.

Some hospitals have shown that the noise can be reduced without any loss of safety. Adjusting limits to the individual patient rather than relying on factory settings removes many false alarms. So does adding a delay of a few seconds, since a large share of alarms correct themselves almost at once. Sending alerts directly to the nurse responsible for a patient, rather than broadcasting them to the whole ward, means that fewer people hear signals that are not meant for them. None of these measures is technically demanding. What they require is a willingness to accept that an alarm which never sounds unnecessarily will occasionally stay silent when it should have sounded, and that this risk may be smaller than the one it replaces.
options: Hospital alarms are often poorly designed because manufacturers ignore nurses' needs.
Nurses have grown careless about responding to the alarms on their wards.
Alarms in intensive care should be replaced by more frequent checks by staff.
Alarms that are each meant to protect patients can together make care less safe.
questions.explain: The first paragraph sets out the thesis: each alarm 'was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer', but 'taken together' they may be doing the opposite; the rest of the text explains how too many signals lead staff to miss real emergencies and how the number could be reduced. Manufacturers' settings are explained by their wish to be protected if something goes wrong, not by indifference to nurses, and they are only part of the problem. The author describes staff as learning 'quite reasonably' that an alarm usually means nothing, which does not amount to calling them careless. And the remedies proposed adjust the alarms rather than replace them with checks by staff.

Monitors beep when a patient's heart rate rises or falls, infusion pumps chime when a bag runs empty, and sensors sound when a clip slips off a finger. Each of these alarms exists for a good reason, and each was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer. Taken together, however, they may be doing the opposite.

The problem is not that alarms fail to go off, but that they go off far too often. Studies of intensive care units have repeatedly found that most alarms require no action at all: the patient has moved, a cable has come loose, or a reading has briefly crossed a limit and returned to normal of its own accord. Staff who hear hundreds of such signals in a shift learn, quite reasonably, that an alarm usually means nothing. They respond more slowly, silence devices without checking, or widen the limits until the machines fall quiet. Nurses call this alarm fatigue, and it has been linked to cases in which a genuine emergency went unnoticed because the signal announcing it sounded exactly like the hundred false ones that preceded it.

What makes the problem stubborn is that no one is responsible for it. A manufacturer who sets a monitor to sound at the slightest irregularity is protected if something goes wrong; a manufacturer who sets it to stay quiet is not. Every individual decision to add an alarm, or to make one more sensitive, is easy to defend. The total, which is what the nurse actually has to live with, is no one's decision at all.

Some hospitals have shown that the noise can be reduced without any loss of safety. Adjusting limits to the individual patient rather than relying on factory settings removes many false alarms. So does adding a delay of a few seconds, since a large share of alarms correct themselves almost at once. Sending alerts directly to the nurse responsible for a patient, rather than broadcasting them to the whole ward, means that fewer people hear signals that are not meant for them. None of these measures is technically demanding. What they require is a willingness to accept that an alarm which never sounds unnecessarily will occasionally stay silent when it should have sounded, and that this risk may be smaller than the one it replaces.
options: New technology that can tell genuine emergencies from false alarms.
Acceptance that a quieter system will occasionally miss a real problem.
Funding for systems that send alerts directly to individual nurses.
Nurses who are willing to change how they respond to alarms.
questions.explain: After listing the measures, the author writes: 'What they require is a willingness to accept that an alarm which never sounds unnecessarily will occasionally stay silent when it should have sounded', a risk that may be smaller than the one it replaces. New technology is not what is needed, since 'none of these measures is technically demanding'. Sending alerts to individual nurses is one of the measures, but the text says nothing about funding being the obstacle. And the changes concern how alarms are set and routed, not how nurses respond to them.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what weakness do some scholars see in the painted reconstructions?
questions.passage:
The white marble statues of ancient Greece and Rome have long stood for a particular ideal of beauty: calm, pure and free of decoration. Yet many of them were never meant to be white. Traces of pigment survive on a great number of ancient sculptures, and with the help of ultraviolet light and chemical analysis researchers have been able to reconstruct patterned clothing, coloured eyes and painted skin. The ancients, it seems, painted their statues, and often brightly.

Reconstructions based on this evidence regularly provoke dismay. Visitors to exhibitions of painted copies have described them as garish, even vulgar, and some scholars have objected that the reconstructions rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork. That objection has some force: a fleck of blue on a fold of drapery does not reveal the exact shade, or how it was combined with other colours. But the discomfort seems to have older roots. The admiration for white marble took shape in the eighteenth century, when the paint had long since weathered away, and writers who knew the statues only in their faded state built a whole theory of classical taste largely on that absence. What looks like a reaction to bad reconstruction may often be loyalty to that theory.
options: Much of what they show cannot be read from the surviving traces of paint.
They use pigments that would not have been available in antiquity.
They may reproduce paint that was added long after the statues were made.
Their colours are brighter than modern visitors find tasteful.
questions.explain: Some scholars object that the reconstructions 'rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork', and the author agrees that a fleck of blue does not reveal the exact shade or how it was combined with other colours; much of what the copies show must therefore be filled in. The text says nothing about anachronistic pigments or about paint added after antiquity. The complaint that the colours are garish comes from visitors, not from the scholars, and concerns taste rather than evidence.

questions.prompt: Which alternative best fits gap 1?
questions.passage:
For most of history, repairing things was not a hobby or a political statement but simply what people did. Shoes were resoled, clothes were patched, and radios went back to the shop when they stopped working. Today the same instinct often meets an obstacle that has little to do with skill. Many products are designed in ways that make repair __1__: batteries are glued in place, parts are fixed with unusual screws, and spare components are sold only to authorised workshops, if at all.

Manufacturers argue that these choices are not meant to discourage repair. Gluing a battery makes a phone thinner, sealing a case keeps out water, and restricting access to parts protects customers from poor workmanship. Some of these arguments are __2__. A sealed phone does survive a fall into a puddle better than one held together with clips. But they explain less than they claim to. A thinner phone does not require that a replacement screen be paired electronically with the original circuit board, so that a perfectly good part fitted by an independent repairer refuses to work.

The movement for a 'right to repair' therefore asks for something quite __3__. It does not demand that products be built to last forever, or that good design give way to durability. It asks that owners and independent workshops have access to the same parts, tools and manuals as the manufacturer's own technicians. __4__, it asks that a product, once bought, should belong to the person who bought it.
questions.explain: The sentence describes an 'obstacle' that has 'little to do with skill', and the examples after the colon (glued batteries, unusual screws, spare parts that are hard to get) all make repairing a product difficult, so the design makes repair 'impractical'. 'Unnecessary' would mean that products no longer need repairing, but the examples hinder repair rather than remove the need for it. 'Hazardous' does not fit, since none of the examples concerns danger to the person doing the repair; the risk to customers mentioned later is poor workmanship. 'Unpopular' would concern people's attitudes, whereas the paragraph is about obstacles built into the products themselves.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the text, had it been difficult to explain the home advantage before 2020?
questions.passage:
For as long as statistics have been kept, teams in most sports have won more often at home than away. Explanations have never been in short supply. Players sleep in their own beds and avoid tiring journeys; they know the quirks of their own pitch; and, above all, they are cheered on by thousands of supporters. Until recently there was no way of separating these factors, because they almost always came together. Then, in 2020, the pandemic forced football leagues across Europe to play their matches in empty stadiums, and researchers suddenly had an experiment they could never have arranged themselves.

The results were striking. In several leagues the home advantage shrank noticeably, and in some it seemed to disappear altogether. More revealing than the size of the change, however, was where it showed up. The way the teams themselves played changed less clearly than one might have expected. What changed most consistently was the behaviour of referees, who in many leagues now showed visiting players fewer yellow cards, relative to home players, than before. The roar of the crowd, it seems, had been working less on the players it was meant to encourage than on the official it was meant to intimidate.

It would be a mistake, though, to treat the matter as settled. The season was hardly normal in other respects: matches were crammed into a short period, travel was restricted, and players were living under unusual rules. Nor did every league show the same pattern, and in a few the home advantage barely changed. And the advantage had in any case been shrinking slowly for decades, perhaps because easier travel and more uniform pitches had eroded some of its older causes. The empty stadiums showed that crowds matter. They could not show how much, or that they matter in the same way everywhere.
options: Statistics on away matches had not been collected systematically.
Researchers disagreed about how the advantage should be measured.
The possible causes were hardly ever found apart from one another.
The advantage differed too much between sports to have a single cause.
questions.explain: The text lists several possible explanations (rest, familiarity with the pitch, supporters) and says there was 'no way of separating these factors, because they almost always came together'. In other words, the possible causes were hardly ever found apart, so their effects could not be told apart either. The empty stadiums of 2020 changed that by removing one of them, the crowds. The text states that statistics have long been kept and says nothing about how they were collected for away matches. No disagreement about measurement is mentioned, and the advantage is described as common to 'most sports', not as differing between them.

questions.prompt: How does the author regard the story about instant cake mix?
questions.passage:
In the 1950s, the story goes, the makers of an instant cake mix found that their product sold poorly until they removed the powdered egg and asked customers to add a fresh one themselves. Having to crack an egg, it was said, made baking feel like baking again. The story is probably too neat to be true; there is little evidence for it, and other explanations for the change in recipe are at least as plausible. But it has survived because it captures something that later experiments have confirmed. People who assemble a piece of flat-pack furniture, fold a paper crane or build a simple model tend to value the result more highly than an identical object made by someone else, and are willing to pay more for it.

The effect has a limit, and the limit is revealing. When participants in such studies built something and then had to take it apart again, or were stopped before they could finish it, the extra value largely disappeared. It is not effort as such that people prize, then, but effort that has visibly paid off.
options: As early evidence of an effect that experiments later confirmed.
As a misleading tale that has distorted later research on the subject.
As doubtful history that nonetheless illustrates a real effect.
As an example of how advertisers exploit customers' wish to take part.
questions.explain: The author calls the story 'probably too neat to be true', with 'little evidence for it', but says it has survived 'because it captures something that later experiments have confirmed'. It is therefore doubtful as history but a fitting illustration. Since the author doubts that it happened, it cannot be treated as early evidence. Nothing suggests that the story has distorted research; on the contrary, the research is said to confirm the idea it captures. And the text does not present the story as an example of advertisers exploiting customers.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by saying that crowd figures are 'easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie'?
questions.passage:
After almost every large demonstration, two numbers appear. The organisers announce one, the police another, and the gap between them is often so wide that it is tempting to assume both are invented. In fact, counting a crowd is not especially mysterious. The standard method, developed in the 1960s, is to divide the area the crowd occupies into sections, estimate how densely people are packed in a sample of them, and multiply. A loosely gathered crowd might have one person per square metre; in a tightly packed one, where people can barely move, there may be four or more.

The arithmetic is simple. The difficulty lies in the inputs, and especially in density, which varies enormously across a single crowd. The area just in front of a stage may be packed solid while the edges are thin, and an estimate that takes the dense centre as typical can easily double the true figure. Marches create a further problem, because people come and go. A count of everyone present at the moment of peak attendance will miss those who joined for an hour and left early, while adding up everyone who passes a given point risks counting the same people twice if the route loops back on itself.

None of this means that the figures are arbitrary, but it does mean that they are easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie. Organisers have an obvious interest in large numbers and authorities sometimes in small ones, and each side can choose, honestly enough, the assumptions that suit it. questions.prompt: Why, according to the text, did Ise once seem 'a puzzle, even a scandal' to many European conservationists?
questions.passage:
At Ise, the most sacred buildings of Japan's most important Shinto shrine are taken down roughly every twenty years and rebuilt, in fresh cypress wood, on a neighbouring plot. The practice has continued, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The buildings a visitor sees today are therefore only a few years old, and yet they are widely regarded as one of the oldest living traditions of Japanese architecture.

To many European conservationists, this once seemed a puzzle, even a scandal. Their own tradition held that what deserves protection is original material: the stones actually laid by medieval masons, the timbers actually cut in the year a church was built. Replacing such material, however faithfully, was thought to destroy precisely what made a building valuable. By that standard, Ise has nothing left to protect.

Yet the rebuilding preserves something that the European approach can lose. Each reconstruction requires carpenters who know the old techniques, and the twenty-year cycle ensures that the knowledge is passed on before those who hold it grow too old to work. A medieval church whose every original beam has been carefully preserved may stand intact while the skills needed to build it have long since vanished. Since the 1990s, international guidelines on heritage have recognised that authenticity can reside in form, use and tradition as well as in material. Ise did not change its practice to fit that view; the view, in part, was changed to make room for Ise.
options: The rebuilding destroyed buildings that had stood for over a thousand years.
The new buildings were not faithful copies of the ones they replaced.
They doubted that the tradition had really continued without interruption.
They located a building's value in the material it was originally made of.
questions.explain: The European tradition held that 'what deserves protection is original material', and that replacing it 'however faithfully' destroys what makes a building valuable; buildings that are replaced every twenty years thus seemed to have 'nothing left to protect'. It is the practice of rebuilding, not the buildings, that is over a thousand years old; each building stands for only about twenty years. The text does not suggest that the new buildings are unfaithful copies, and the phrase 'however faithfully' shows that even faithful copies would not have satisfied the European view. The interruptions are mentioned by the author and are not presented as the source of the conservationists' objection.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Economists who want to show that markets can lock in an inferior technology have for decades reached for the same example: the keyboard on which this text was typed. The QWERTY layout, the story goes, was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters whose type bars jammed when neighbouring keys were struck in quick succession, and it deliberately separated common pairs of letters in order to slow typists down. The jamming problem disappeared long ago, and in the 1930s an American educational psychologist, August Dvorak, patented a layout that placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, directly under the typist's fingers. Tests showed that typists trained on it worked dramatically faster. Yet QWERTY survived, because everyone had learned it, every machine used it, and no one could afford to be the first to switch.

It is an elegant story, and its lesson, that an early accident can become permanent even when something better is available, has been applied to everything from video formats to railway gauges. In an influential paper in the 1980s, the economist Paul David used it to argue that history matters to economics in a way that standard models had overlooked: the path a market takes can determine where it ends up.

The difficulty is that almost every part of the story has been questioned. The claim that QWERTY was designed to slow typists down rests on thin evidence; the arrangement seems to have emerged from a long series of practical adjustments, among them attempts to reduce jamming, and fewer jams may well have made typists faster rather than slower. More seriously, the tests that showed Dvorak's layout to be far superior were, for the most part, carried out or supervised by Dvorak himself, who had a patent to sell. A later study run by the United States government in the 1950s found that retraining experienced typists on the new layout brought gains too small to justify the cost, and later comparisons have generally found the differences to be modest.

If that is right, the keyboard is not an example of a market trapped with an inferior product, but of a market that declined to pay for an improvement too small to be worth the trouble. That would be a rather different lesson, and a less dramatic one.

Defenders of the original argument have a reasonable reply. Path dependence, they point out, never required the losing technology to be dramatically better; it only requires that early choices constrain later ones, which in the case of the keyboard they plainly do. Nobody who learned to type on QWERTY is eager to start again. That is true, but it rather changes the subject. What made the keyboard such a powerful illustration was not the modest claim that habits are costly to change, which few would dispute, but the stronger claim that whole markets can be stuck with a clearly worse choice. For that claim the keyboard, it now seems, is a weak witness.

None of this shows that markets never lock in inferior technologies. It shows something narrower and perhaps more useful: that a story can become famous because it illustrates an idea well, and then be cited as evidence for the idea it was chosen to illustrate. The more perfectly an example fits a theory, the more carefully it may deserve to be checked.
options: The idea that markets can lock in inferior technologies has been shown to be mistaken.
The keyboard gives far weaker support to the idea of lock-in than its fame suggests.
QWERTY survived because it was in fact better suited to typing than its rivals.
Economists have exaggerated how costly it is for typists to learn a new layout.
questions.explain: The author shows that most parts of the famous keyboard story have been questioned and concludes that, for the claim that markets can be stuck with a clearly worse choice, the keyboard 'is a weak witness'. The author explicitly says that 'none of this shows that markets never lock in inferior technologies', so the idea itself is not rejected. The text does not claim that QWERTY is better; the critics' view is that the alternative offered only a small improvement. And the cost of relearning is not said to be exaggerated: the government study found the gains too small to justify that cost, and the author accepts that habits are 'costly to change'.

What made the keyboard such a powerful illustration was not the modest claim that habits are costly to change, which few would dispute, but the stronger claim that whole markets can be stuck with a clearly worse choice. For that claim the keyboard, it now seems, is a weak witness.

None of this shows that markets never lock in inferior technologies. It shows something narrower and perhaps more useful: that a story can become famous because it illustrates an idea well, and then be cited as evidence for the idea it was chosen to illustrate. The more perfectly an example fits a theory, the more carefully it may deserve to be checked.

An example can come to count as evidence because it illustrates a theory so well.
Little-known examples are usually more reliable than famous ones.
